claim: The spiking activity of populations of cortical neurons is well described by the dynamics of a small number of population-wide covariance patterns.
source: The spiking activity of populations of cortical neurons is well described by the dynamics of a small number of population-wide covariance patterns, whose activation we refer to as 'latent dynamics'.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established understanding in the field.

claim: Latent dynamics are largely driven by the same correlated synaptic currents across the circuit that determine the generation of local field potentials (LFPs).
source: These latent dynamics are largely driven by the same correlated synaptic currents across the circuit that determine the generation of local field potentials (LFPs).
evidence: This statement is based on biophysical understanding of LFP generation and neural population dynamics.

claim: The correlation between latent dynamics and LFPs was frequency-dependent and varied across regions.
source: The correlation between latent dynamics and LFPs was frequency-dependent and varied across regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: For any given region, the LFP-latent dynamics relationship remained stable throughout the behaviour.
source: However, for any given region, this relationship remained stable throughout the behaviour: in each of primary motor and premotor cortices, the LFP-latent dynamics correlation profile was remarkably similar between movement planning and execution.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated with data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: In primary motor and premotor cortices, the LFP-latent dynamics correlation profile was remarkably similar between movement planning and execution.
source: in each of primary motor and premotor cortices, the LFP-latent dynamics correlation profile was remarkably similar between movement planning and execution.
evidence: This is a specific finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: LFPs result from synaptic currents summed across many thousands of neurons.
source: These same electrodes can also capture the lower frequency local field potentials (LFPs) that result from synaptic currents summed across many thousands of neurons (Mitzdorf, 1985; Einevoll et al., 2013; Lindén et al., 2011; Buzsáki et al., 2012; Pesaran et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to established literature on LFP biophysics.

claim: The spiking activity of neural populations can be well characterised by dynamics of relatively few covariance patterns.
source: The spiking activity of neural populations can be well characterised by dynamics of relatively few covariance patterns (Vyas et al., 2020; Gallego et al., 2017), which we refer to as the 'latent dynamics' (Pandarinath et al., 2018; Gallego et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work establishing this concept.

claim: Studying latent dynamics has provided insight into aspects of animal behaviour including decision making.
source: Studying these latent dynamics has provided insight into aspects of animal behaviour that was not apparent from the activity of single neurons alone, including decision making (Machens et al., 2010; Mante et al., 2013), movement planning (Churchland et al., 2010; Kaufman et al., 2014; Dekleva et al., 2018), learning (Sadtler et al., 2014; Oby et al., 2019; Perich et al., 2018; Vyas et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2020), the control timing (Dekleva et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018b; Remington et al., 2018), and production of consistent behaviour (Gallego et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The latent dynamics are constrained by the neural covariance structure, which is shaped in part by circuit connectivity.
source: The latent dynamics are constrained by the neural covariance structure, which is shaped in part by circuit connectivity (Sadtler et al., 2014; Oby et al., 2019; Okun et al., 2015; Feulner and Clopath, 2021; Feulner et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on neural covariance and connectivity.

claim: Currents through circuit connections and other biophysical properties are the main contributors to the generation of LFPs.
source: Currents through these same connections as well as other biophysical properties of the circuit are the main contributors to the generation of the LFPs (Mitzdorf, 1985; Einevoll et al., 2013; Lindén et al., 2011; Buzsáki et al., 2012; Pesaran et al., 2018; Figure 1A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to LFP biophysics literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Correlations in the synaptic input currents across the population yield changes in LFP power at specific frequency bands.
source: In particular, correlations in the synaptic input currents across the population yield changes in LFP power at specific frequency bands, which often relate to specific brain functions (Buschman et al., 2012; Tremblay et al., 2015; Liu and Newsome, 2006; Pesaran et al., 2002; Scherberger et al., 2005; Gail et al., 2004; Holmes et al., 2018; Sanes and Donoghue, 1993; Zhuang et al., 2010; Bansal et al., 2012; Flint et al., 2012; Stavisky et al., 2015; Perel et al., 2015; Baker et al., 1997; Witham et al., 2010; Witham and Baker, 2012; Buzsáki, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by extensive citations to previous work on LFP frequency bands and brain function.

claim: In motor cortices, movement-related information lies primarily at low and high frequencies (i.e., <5 Hz and >50 Hz).
source: For example, in the motor cortices, movement-related information lies primarily at low and high frequencies (Zhuang et al., 2010; Bansal et al., 2012; Flint et al., 2012; Stavisky et al., 2015) (i.e., <5 Hz and >50 Hz), yet, the clearest LFP signature of imminent movement initiation is a marked decrease in activity in the 15–30 Hz band (Sanes and Donoghue, 1993; Perel et al., 2015; Donoghue et al., 1998; Witham et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies on motor cortex LFPs.

claim: The clearest LFP signature of imminent movement initiation is a marked decrease in activity in the 15–30 Hz band.
source: yet, the clearest LFP signature of imminent movement initiation is a marked decrease in activity in the 15–30 Hz band (Sanes and Donoghue, 1993; Perel et al., 2015; Donoghue et al., 1998; Witham et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies on motor cortex LFPs.

claim: In somatosensory cortical areas 2 and 3a, the 15–30 Hz band contains signatures potentially related to afferent input from the limb.
source: In somatosensory cortical areas 2 and 3a, this same 15–30 Hz band contains signatures potentially related to afferent input from the limb (Witham et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work on somatosensory cortex LFPs.

claim: Region-specific LFP phenomena likely relate to the neural population latent dynamics of each region, as they are both ultimately driven by the same synaptic currents.
source: It seems likely that these region-specific LFP phenomena relate to the neural population latent dynamics of each region, as they are both ultimately driven by the same synaptic currents.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction based on inference from biophysical principles.

claim: Previous studies investigated the relationship between single neuron activity and LFPs.
source: Previous studies investigated the relationship between single neuron activity and LFPs (Pesaran et al., 2002; Perel et al., 2015; Witham and Baker, 2012; Ray et al., 2008; Ray and Maunsell, 2011; Rule et al., 2017; Murthy and Fetz, 1996b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is a lack of a systematic description of how different LFP bands relate to the latent dynamics reflecting the coordinated activity of neural populations driving behaviour.
source: However, we lack a systematic description of how the different LFP bands relate to the latent dynamics reflecting the coordinated activity of the neural populations driving behaviour.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Both LFP and latent dynamics are likely shaped by circuit biophysics.
source: First, since both LFP (Mitzdorf, 1985; Einevoll et al., 2013; Lindén et al., 2011; Buzsáki et al., 2012; Pesaran et al., 2018) and latent dynamics (Sadtler et al., 2014; Oby et al., 2019; Okun et al., 2015) are likely shaped by the circuit biophysics (Figure 1B), we expect to find a robust relationship between these two signals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The relationship between LFPs and latent dynamics should be frequency-dependent.
source: Second, we anticipate finding fundamental differences across LFP bands since only a specific subset of them is correlated with behaviour for any given brain region (Buschman et al., 2012; Tremblay et al., 2015; Liu and Newsome, 2006; Pesaran et al., 2002; Scherberger et al., 2005; Gail et al., 2004; Holmes et al., 2018; Sanes and Donoghue, 1993; Zhuang et al., 2010; Bansal et al., 2012; Flint et al., 2012; Stavisky et al., 2015; Perel et al., 2015; Baker et al., 1997; Witham et al., 2010; Witham and Baker, 2012; Buzsáki, 2002; Murthy and Fetz, 1996a). That is, the relationship between LFPs and latent dynamics should be frequency-dependent.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: As long as circuit biophysics remain unchanged, the LFP-latent dynamics associations will remain similarly stable.
source: Third, we expect that as long as circuit biophysics remain unchanged, the LFP-latent dynamics associations will remain similarly stable.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction based on inference about circuit properties.

claim: The various associations between motor cortical LFPs and latent dynamics should not change in the short time scale spanning the preparation and execution of a movement.
source: Thus, the various associations between motor cortical LFPs and latent dynamics should not change in the short time scale spanning the preparation and execution of a movement.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction based on inference about circuit stability.

claim: Different sensorimotor cortical areas have important differences in inputs and function.
source: Lastly, since different sensorimotor cortical areas have important differences in inputs and function (Kakei et al., 2001; Scott, 2012; Cisek and Kalaska, 2010; Das and Fiete, 2020), as well as cytoarchitecture (Hutsler et al., 2005; Dum and Strick, 1991), we hypothesise that the relationships between LFPs and latent dynamics should be region-specific.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on cortical area differences.

claim: The relationships between LFPs and latent dynamics should be region-specific.
source: we hypothesise that the relationships between LFPs and latent dynamics should be region-specific.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction based on known differences in cortical areas.

claim: Primary motor cortex (M1) is the main cortical output that controls movement execution.
source: (1) primary motor cortex (M1), the main cortical output that controls movement execution (Rathelot and Strick, 2006; Fetz and Cheney, 1980; Morrow and Miller, 2003; Sergio et al., 2005);
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on M1 function.

claim: Dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) is a region that integrates inputs from many structures and is largely involved in movement planning.
source: (2) dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), a region that integrates inputs from many structures and is largely involved in movement planning (Dekleva et al., 2018; Shen and Alexander, 1997a; Santhanam et al., 2009; Crammond and Kalaska, 1994);
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on PMd function.

claim: Area 2 of somatosensory cortex is where multimodal proprioceptive and cutaneous information about the state of the limb is processed.
source: and (3) area 2 of somatosensory cortex, where multimodal proprioceptive and cutaneous information about the state of the limb is processed (Chowdhury et al., 2020; London and Miller, 2013; Pons et al., 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on area 2 function.

claim: The relationship between the LFPs and the latent dynamics from the same cortical region is frequency-dependent and varies across cortical regions.
source: Our results show that the relationship between the LFPs and the latent dynamics from the same cortical region is indeed frequency-dependent and varies across cortical regions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The region-specific LFP-latent dynamics 'correlation profiles' remain remarkably stable across the evolving processes mediating movement planning and execution.
source: Yet, the region-specific LFP-latent dynamics 'correlation profiles' remain remarkably stable across the evolving processes mediating movement planning and execution (Dekleva et al., 2018; Shen and Alexander, 1997b; Ames et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The LFP-latent dynamics relationships do not trivially arise from correlations between single unit firing rates and LFP recordings from the same intracortical electrode.
source: Finally, we show that these relationships do not trivially arise from correlations between single unit firing rates and LFP recordings from the same intracortical electrode; instead, they reflect the coordinated activity of neural populations.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: The LFP-latent dynamics relationships reflect the coordinated activity of neural populations.
source: instead, they reflect the coordinated activity of neural populations.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: The LFP-latent dynamics relationships hold both during movement execution and as animals perform more 'abstract computations' related to movement planning.
source: This holds both during movement execution and as animals perform more 'abstract computations' related to movement planning.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: LFP bands relate to the latent dynamics in a stable, region-specific, and frequency-dependent manner.
source: These results, which are critical for bridging studies of the sensorimotor system that use LFPs and neural population activity, paint a picture in which LFP bands relate to the latent dynamics in a stable, region-specific, and frequency-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings stated in the introduction.

claim: Some LFP bands are strongly correlated with latent dynamics yet carry little information about the animal's movement.
source: This picture has one unexpected feature: some LFP bands are strongly correlated with latent dynamics yet carry little information about the animal's movement.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Low-dimensional latent dynamics have been found across many brain regions.
source: Given that low-dimensional latent dynamics have been found across many brain regions (Gallego et al., 2017; Keemink and Machens, 2019), our findings are likely to translate beyond the sensorimotor system.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on latent dynamics in different brain regions.

claim: The findings are likely to translate beyond the sensorimotor system.
source: our findings are likely to translate beyond the sensorimotor system.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the generality of latent dynamics across brain regions.

claim: Four monkeys were trained to perform an instructed delay centre-out reaching task using a manipulandum.
source: We trained four monkeys (C, M, H, and L) to perform an instructed delay centre-out reaching task using a manipulandum (Figure 2A) (Methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and is illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Monkeys started each trial by holding a cursor in the central target before one of the eight outer targets was presented.
source: The monkeys started each trial by holding a cursor in the central target before one of the eight outer targets was presented.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task procedure.

claim: After a variable delay period, an auditory 'go cue' instructed monkeys to move the cursor towards the presented target.
source: After a variable delay period, an auditory 'go cue' instructed them to move the cursor towards the presented target.
evidence: This describes the behavioral task procedure.

claim: For monkeys with implants in area 2 (Monkeys H and L), both the delay and holding periods were omitted.
source: For the monkeys with implants in area 2 (Monkeys H and L), both the delay and holding periods were omitted.
evidence: This describes a modification to the behavioral task for specific monkeys.

claim: Each monkey was implanted with one or two 96-channel microelectrode arrays.
source: Each monkey was implanted with one or two 96-channel microelectrode arrays (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the recording setup and is illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: Monkeys C and M had dual implants in the arm regions of M1 and PMd.
source: Monkeys C and M had dual implants in the arm regions of M1 and PMd, whereas Monkeys H and L had a single implant in the arm region of area 2.
evidence: This describes the implant locations for different monkeys.

claim: Monkeys H and L had a single implant in the arm region of area 2.
source: whereas Monkeys H and L had a single implant in the arm region of area 2.
evidence: This describes the implant locations for specific monkeys.

claim: Neural spiking and LFP were simultaneously recorded on each electrode.
source: We simultaneously recorded neural spiking and LFP on each electrode.
evidence: This describes the recording methodology.

claim: The spiking signals were manually sorted to identify putative single neurons.
source: The spiking signals were manually sorted to identify putative single neurons (Figure 2D).
evidence: This describes the spike sorting procedure and is illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to find the lower-dimensional neural manifold spanning the dominant population-wide activity patterns.
source: We used principal component analysis (PCA) to find the lower-dimensional neural manifold spanning the dominant population-wide activity patterns (Gallego et al., 2017; Cunningham and Yu, 2019) choosing the following manifold dimensionalities based on previous studies (Gallego et al., 2020; Churchland et al., 2010; Perich et al., 2018): 10 dimensions for M1, 15 for PMd, and 8 dimensions for area 2.
evidence: This describes the analysis method used to compute latent dynamics, supported by citations.

claim: The manifold dimensionalities chosen were 10 dimensions for M1, 15 for PMd, and 8 dimensions for area 2.
source: choosing the following manifold dimensionalities based on previous studies (Gallego et al., 2020; Churchland et al., 2010; Perich et al., 2018): 10 dimensions for M1, 15 for PMd, and 8 dimensions for area 2.
evidence: This describes the specific dimensionalities used, based on previous studies.

claim: LFP power was calculated in eight standard frequency bands: 0.5–4 Hz, 4–8 Hz, 8–12 Hz, 12–25 Hz, 25–50 Hz, 50–100 Hz, 100–200 Hz, and 200–400 Hz.
source: We calculated the LFP power in eight standard frequency bands (Bansal et al., 2012; Flint et al., 2012; Stavisky et al., 2015; Zhuang et al., 2010): 0.5–4 Hz, 4–8 Hz, 8–12 Hz, 12–25 Hz, 25–50 Hz, 50–100 Hz, 100–200 Hz, and 200–400 Hz for each electrode from which we could record at least one neuron.
evidence: This describes the LFP processing methodology, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The local motor potential (LMP) captures fluctuations in total LFP power.
source: We also computed the local motor potential (LMP), which captures fluctuations in total LFP power (Flint et al., 2012; Stavisky et al., 2015; Figure 2F).
evidence: This describes the LMP computation, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2F.

claim: The relationship between M1 latent dynamics and each of the LFP frequency bands was frequency-dependent.
source: We found that the relationship between LFPs and latent dynamics was both consistent across subjects and frequency-dependent: there were clear correlations between LFP and latent dynamics in the low and high bands (median correlation: 0.3–0.6), whereas the correlations approached zero in the mid-range bands (8–50 Hz) (coloured distributions in Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 summarises all datasets).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B and supplementary figures.

claim: There were clear correlations between LFP and latent dynamics in the low and high bands (median correlation: 0.3–0.6).
source: there were clear correlations between LFP and latent dynamics in the low and high bands (median correlation: 0.3–0.6)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The correlations between LFP and latent dynamics approached zero in the mid-range bands (8–50 Hz).
source: whereas the correlations approached zero in the mid-range bands (8–50 Hz)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The frequency-dependent LFP-latent dynamics correlations were stable across sessions.
source: Importantly, these frequency-dependent LFP-latent dynamics correlations were also stable across sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Surrogate neural firing rates generated using tensor maximum entropy (TME) preserved the covariance across neurons but had different covariance across trials and over time than the actual data.
source: Here, we used TME to generate surrogate neural firing rates that preserved the covariance across neurons but that had different covariance across trials and over time (i.e., different dynamics) than the actual data.
evidence: This describes the control analysis methodology.

claim: The surrogate correlations were significantly lower than the actual correlations (median ≤0.1; p<0.001).
source: As predicted, the surrogate correlations were significantly lower than the actual correlations (median ≤0.1; p<0.001 for all comparisons, two-sided Wilcoxon's rank sum test; compare the black and coloured distributions in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the control analysis, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The difference in LFP-latent dynamics correlations across LFP frequencies could not be trivially explained by similar spectral characteristics between the signals.
source: Thus, the difference in LFP-latent dynamics correlations across LFP frequencies could not be trivially explained by similar spectral characteristics between the signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analysis with surrogate data.

claim: Similar LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles were obtained for different manifold dimensionalities.
source: We obtained similar LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles for different manifold dimensionalities (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Similar results were obtained when pooling all putative single neurons on an electrode into 'multi-units'.
source: and when pooling all putative single neurons on an electrode into 'multi-units' (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The results held when modifying the specific frequency bands used for LFP pre-processing within reasonable intervals.
source: Our results also held when modifying the specific frequency bands used for LFP pre-processing within reasonable intervals (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B)
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The results could not be explained by differences in LFP variance across bands.
source: and could not be explained by differences in LFP variance across bands (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C), or by differences in the LFP-LFP relationship across bands (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Latent LFP signals had the same frequency-dependent relationship with the neural population latent dynamics as the full-dimensional LFP power in each channel.
source: These latent LFP signals had the same frequency-dependent relationship with the neural population latent dynamics as the full-dimensional LFP power in each channel (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: M1 latent dynamics allow accurate prediction or 'decoding' of movement kinematics.
source: M1 latent dynamics (Pandarinath et al., 2018; Gallego et al., 2020) and some LFP bands (Zhuang et al., 2010; Bansal et al., 2012; Flint et al., 2012; Stavisky et al., 2015) allow accurate prediction or 'decoding' of movement kinematics.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Some LFP bands allow accurate prediction or 'decoding' of movement kinematics.
source: M1 latent dynamics (Pandarinath et al., 2018; Gallego et al., 2020) and some LFP bands (Zhuang et al., 2010; Bansal et al., 2012; Flint et al., 2012; Stavisky et al., 2015) allow accurate prediction or 'decoding' of movement kinematics.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Decoding accuracy varied considerably across LFP bands, with some (e.g., the LMP and 200–400 Hz) being nearly as predictive as the latent dynamics.
source: Decoding accuracy varied considerably across LFP bands, with some (e.g., the LMP and 200–400 Hz) being nearly as predictive as the latent dynamics (Figure 4B and C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and supplementary figures.

claim: The accuracy of each LFP band was strongly correlated with its similarity to the latent dynamics (R2=0.78; p<0.001).
source: The accuracy of each LFP band was strongly correlated with its similarity to the latent dynamics (R2=0.78; p<0.001, F-test; see Figure 4D)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All of the accurate decoders made similar predictions (pairwise correlation: >0.6).
source: and all of the accurate decoders made similar predictions (pairwise correlation: >0.6; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The predictive accuracy of an LFP band did not depend on its variance.
source: However, the predictive accuracy of an LFP band did not depend on its variance, since it was similar across all bands (Figure 3—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Predicting hand velocity from individual LFP channels was notably worse than predicting from all the channels.
source: Predicting hand velocity from individual LFP channels was notably worse than predicting from all the channels (compare Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; also see Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This finding is supported by comparing data shown in Figure 4C and supplementary figures.

claim: For M1, the relationship between LFP power and latent dynamics varies across frequency bands and predicts how strongly each band relates to the ongoing motor output.
source: Thus, for M1, the relationship between LFP power and latent dynamics varies across frequency bands and predicts how strongly each band relates to the ongoing motor output.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analysis results.

claim: The LFP-latent dynamics correlation profile was virtually identical between movement planning and execution in M1.
source: Repeating the previous CCA alignment procedure for the instructed delay epoch showed that the LFP-latent dynamics correlation profile was virtually identical between movement planning and execution (Figure 5A): a correlation analysis between all pairs of LFP-latent dynamics correlations across all frequency bands, sessions, and monkeys revealed a strong linear association (R2=0.87; p<0.001, F-test; Figure 5B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: A correlation analysis between all pairs of LFP-latent dynamics correlations across all frequency bands, sessions, and monkeys revealed a strong linear association (R2=0.87; p<0.001) between movement planning and execution.
source: a correlation analysis between all pairs of LFP-latent dynamics correlations across all frequency bands, sessions, and monkeys revealed a strong linear association (R2=0.87; p<0.001, F-test; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: During the inter-trial interval, M1 is not actively engaged in movement generation so neurons typically fire less.
source: In this period, M1 is not actively engaged in movement generation so neurons typically fire less (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: During the inter-trial interval, M1 neurons become less correlated.
source: and become less correlated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The LFP-latent dynamics correlations decreased during the inter-trial intervals compared to movement execution.
source: As expected, the correlations indeed became much lower during the inter-trial intervals than during movement execution (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: The observation that the LFP-latent dynamics correlation profile remains preserved between movement planning and execution indicates that the observed association is not a trivial epiphenomenal consequence of the frequency content of movement.
source: The observation that the LFP-latent dynamics correlation profile remains preserved between movement planning and execution extends our previous findings to a more abstract process occurring in the absence of movement. It also indicates that the observed association is not a trivial epiphenomenal consequence of the frequency content of movement, but instead likely reflects underlying physiological processes related to the production of behaviourally relevant neural activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the stability across behavioral epochs.

claim: The decrease in LFP-latent dynamics correlations during the inter-trial intervals provides additional support for the interpretation that the association reflects underlying physiological processes.
source: The decrease in LFP-latent dynamics correlations during the inter-trial intervals provides additional support for this interpretation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the decrease during inter-trial intervals.

claim: PMd is a 'higher' motor region with a different cytoarchitecture from M1 thought to be key for planning an action.
source: We studied PMd, a 'higher' motor region with a different cytoarchitecture from M1 (Dum and Strick, 1991) thought to be key for planning an action (Dekleva et al., 2018; Crammond and Kalaska, 1994; Shen and Alexander, 1997b; Ohbayashi et al., 2016; Churchland and Shenoy, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on PMd structure and function.

claim: In PMd, the LFP-latent dynamics correlations were markedly frequency-dependent.
source: As for M1, the LFP-latent dynamics correlations were markedly frequency-dependent (Figure 6B)
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In PMd, LFP-latent dynamics correlations were much stronger in the low and high frequencies, greatly exceeding the surrogate control (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
source: much stronger in the low and high frequencies, for which they greatly exceeded the surrogate control (two-sided Wilcoxon's rank sum test, p<0.001 for all comparisons).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Virtually all PMd datasets (10 of 12) exhibited a strong correlation at 12–25 Hz, which was notably absent in M1.
source: Interestingly, virtually all the datasets (10 of 12; pooled results in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) exhibited a strong correlation at 12–25 Hz, which was notably absent in M1 despite the two regions having similar power spectra (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), as well as power spectral density (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B) and variance (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) in each LFP band.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and supplementary figures.

claim: PMd and M1 have similar power spectra.
source: despite the two regions having similar power spectra (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), as well as power spectral density (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B) and variance (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) in each LFP band.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The LFP-latent dynamics correlation profile in PMd was stable between movement planning and execution (R2=0.79; p<0.001).
source: Thus, we tested whether the LFP-latent dynamics correlation profile was preserved as in M1, and found it to be stable between movement planning and execution (R2=0.79; p<0.001, F-test; Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2D, E show that LFP power remains constant across these two epochs too).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: During the inter-trial period in PMd, the correlations dropped, though less markedly than for M1.
source: During the inter-trial period when PMd neurons become less active, the correlations dropped, though less markedly than for M1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The frequency-dependent relationship between LFPs and latent dynamics changes across cortical regions but, within a region, remains stable across different behaviour-related processes those regions are involved in.
source: Therefore, the frequency-dependent relationship between LFPs and latent dynamics changes across cortical regions but, within a region, remains stable across different behaviour-related processes those regions are involved in.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing M1 and PMd results.

claim: The performance of classifiers that predicted the upcoming target from PMd instructed delay activity varied dramatically across LFP bands.
source: The performance of classifiers that predicted the upcoming target from the instructed delay activity (Gallego et al., 2020; Santhanam et al., 2009) (Methods) varied dramatically across LFP bands (Figure 6E; individual examples in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and supplementary figures.

claim: High-frequency LFP bands in PMd were almost as accurate as the latent dynamics in predicting the upcoming target.
source: high-frequency bands were almost as accurate as the latent dynamics
evidence: This finding is from the classification analysis of PMd data.

claim: Low-frequency LFP bands in PMd had worse and more variable prediction accuracy across monkeys (~50% accuracy for Monkey C; close to chance for Monkey M).
source: while classifier accuracy at low frequencies was worse and quite variable across monkeys (~50% accuracy for Monkey C; close to chance for Monkey M).
evidence: This finding is from the classification analysis of PMd data.

claim: Not all PMd LFP bands that were significantly correlated with the latent dynamics also predicted the upcoming target.
source: Interestingly, not all bands that were significantly correlated with the latent dynamics also predicted the upcoming target (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C); most notably, despite being among the most correlated bands, 12–25 Hz prediction accuracy was barely above chance.
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Despite being among the most correlated bands in PMd, 12–25 Hz prediction accuracy was barely above chance.
source: most notably, despite being among the most correlated bands, 12–25 Hz prediction accuracy was barely above chance.
evidence: This finding is from the classification analysis of PMd data.

claim: Oscillations in area 2 of somatosensory cortex likely reflect somatosensory feedback processing.
source: While LFPs in PMd and M1 primarily relate to preparing and generating movement, oscillations in area 2 of somatosensory cortex likely reflect somatosensory feedback processing (Witham et al., 2007; Baker et al., 2006), perhaps in combination with efference copy signals (Witham et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on area 2 function.

claim: Both the low- and high-frequency LFP bands of area 2 were strongly correlated with the latent dynamics (p<0.001 for all comparisons).
source: Both the low- and high-frequency LFP bands of area 2 were strongly correlated with the latent dynamics (Figure 7B; two-sided Wilcoxon's rank sum test, p<0.001 for all comparisons; pooled results in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Area 2 exhibited a strong, significant correlation at 12–25 Hz (and for Monkey H also at 25–50 Hz), which was previously observed in PMd but not in M1.
source: Intriguingly, we observed a strong, significant correlation at 12–25 Hz (and for Monkey H also at 25–50 Hz), which we previously observed in PMd but not in M1.
evidence: This finding is from the area 2 data analysis.

claim: All area 2 LFP-latent dynamics correlations dropped dramatically during the inter-trial period.
source: Again, all LFP-latent dynamics correlations dropped dramatically during the inter-trial period (Figure 7C), when monkeys did not move, and area 2 neurons go practically silent (London and Miller, 2013).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 7C and a citation to previous work.

claim: During the inter-trial period, area 2 neurons go practically silent.
source: when monkeys did not move, and area 2 neurons go practically silent (London and Miller, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In area 2, the low- and high-frequency bands provided the best predictions of movement.
source: As was the case for M1, the low- and high-frequency bands provided the best predictions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: In area 2, contrary to M1 (though similar to PMd), the strength of the correlation between an LFP band and the latent dynamics did not predict how well that band could be used to decode movement.
source: Yet, contrary to M1 (though similar to PMd), the strength of the correlation between an LFP band and the latent dynamics did not predict how well that band could be used to decode movement (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Robust region-specific LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles remain stable for different processes underlying behaviour.
source: Therefore, we have found robust region-specific LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles that remain stable for different processes underlying behaviour (Figures 3B, 6B and 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The correspondence between LFP-latent dynamics correlations and behavioural decoding is strongest for M1.
source: and whose correspondence to behavioural decoding is strongest for M1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing decoding results across regions.

claim: Most within-electrode correlations between LFPs and single neuron firing rates for M1, PMd, and area 2 were very low, statistically no different from the across-electrode correlations.
source: In fact, most within-electrode correlations for M1, PMd, and area 2 were very low, statistically no different from the across-electrode correlations (two-sided Wilcoxon's rank sum test, p≥0.1, except for M1 LMP (p=0.03) and 0.5–4 Hz (p=0.05); Figure 8A)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the control analysis, shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The observed similarities between LFPs and latent dynamics cannot be predicted from the single neuron activity.
source: suggesting that the observed similarities between LFPs and latent dynamics cannot be predicted from the single neuron activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analysis comparing within- and across-electrode correlations.

claim: The LFP-latent dynamics correlations are always much lower than the LFP-single neuron correlations.
source: Notably, the LFP-single neuron correlations were always much lower than the LFP-latent dynamics correlations (Figure 8B).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: There was a linear association between LFP-latent dynamics correlations and LFP-single neuron correlations (R2=0.54; p<0.001) but the slope was very low (ß1=0.15).
source: Although there was a linear association between the two (R2=0.54; p<0.001, F-test) the slope was very low (ß1=0.15), which indicates that even for high LFP-latent dynamics correlations, the LFP-single neuron correlations were still rather weak.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the control analysis.

claim: The LFP-single neuron activity correlations remained low after 'denoising' the single neuron firing rates by subtracting their projection outside the neural manifold.
source: The LFP-single neuron activity correlations remained low after we 'denoised' the single neuron firing rates by subtracting their projection outside the neural manifold, seeking to eliminate the components of the single neuron activity that are not shared across the population (Methods) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Combining all the neurons on the same electrode as 'multi-units' did not change the results.
source: Combining all the neurons on the same electrode as 'multi-units' also did not change the results (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This finding is supported by data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Specific LFP bands capture population-wide features of the latent dynamics that contribute to their generation in a region-specific, stable manner.
source: These controls show that specific LFP bands capture population-wide features of the latent dynamics that contribute to their generation in a region-specific, stable manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analyses.

claim: Changes in power within specific LFP frequency bands correlate well with behavioural and cognitive processes such as initiating a movement.
source: LFPs are intriguing neural signals: changes in power within specific LFP frequency bands correlate well with behavioural and cognitive processes such as initiating a movement (Sanes and Donoghue, 1993; Perel et al., 2015; Donoghue et al., 1998; Witham et al., 2007; O'Leary and Hatsopoulos, 2006) or choosing among different stimulus-response rules (Buschman et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on LFP correlates of behavior.

claim: The relationship between LFPs and the activity of neurons driving behavioral processes has long been elusive.
source: yet their relationship with the activity of the neurons driving these processes has long been elusive.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in understanding that the current study addresses.

claim: LFP biophysics are determined by circuit architecture and the correlation among synaptic inputs to neural populations.
source: LFP biophysics are determined by circuit architecture (Einevoll et al., 2013) and the correlation among synaptic inputs to neural populations (Lindén et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on LFP biophysics.

claim: Circuit architecture and correlation among synaptic inputs also help define the neural covariance structure and shape the latent dynamics.
source: Since both of these also help define the neural covariance structure and shape the latent dynamics, we hypothesised that there should be a fundamental relationship between LFPs and latent dynamics.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from biophysical principles.

claim: Associations between LFPs and latent dynamics are stable and frequency-dependent for each of three different regions of monkey sensorimotor cortex.
source: Here, we report, for each of three different regions of monkey sensorimotor cortex, that associations between LFPs and latent dynamics are stable and frequency-dependent (Figures 3B, 6B and 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the discussion and supported by data in multiple figures.

claim: LFP-latent dynamics associations are region-specific, as expected if main function and circuit biophysics play a role in determining them.
source: They are also region-specific, as expected if main function and circuit biophysics play a role in determining them.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing results across regions.

claim: Previous studies spanning a broad range of regions present a puzzling story in which only the medium-high frequency LFPs (typically, 40–80 Hz) are associated with the activity of single neurons or multi-units.
source: Spanning a broad range of regions, from primary visual to motor cortices, they present a puzzling story in which only the medium-high frequency LFPs (typically, 40–80 Hz) are associated with the activity of single neurons or multi-units (Pesaran et al., 2002; Perel et al., 2015; Witham and Baker, 2012; Ray et al., 2008; Ray and Maunsell, 2011; Rule et al., 2017; Murthy and Fetz, 1996b).
evidence: This statement summarizes previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: The lack of single neuron-LFP correlations at low frequencies seems at odds with biophysical models predicting shared synaptic inputs to be most strongly represented in the low-frequency LFPs.
source: The lack of single neuron-LFP correlations at low frequencies seems at odds with biophysical models predicting shared synaptic inputs – expected to drive single neuron activity – to be most strongly represented in the low-frequency LFPs (Łęski et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement identifies an apparent contradiction in the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Studies of M1 multielectrode LFP recordings show that both the high-frequency and low-frequency LFPs allow muscle activity and movement kinematics to be decoded accurately.
source: Studies of M1 multielectrode LFP recordings align better with this prediction, since both the high-frequency and low-frequency LFPs allow muscle activity (Flint et al., 2012) and movement kinematics (Bansal et al., 2012; Stavisky et al., 2015) to be decoded accurately (Figure 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The ability to predict behaviour from the low-frequency LFPs hints at a relationship between LFPs and neural population activity.
source: Assuming that a large component of the firing of M1 neural populations relates to the motor commands, the ability to predict behaviour from the low-frequency LFPs hints at a relationship between the two.
evidence: This is an inference based on the decoding results and known M1 function.

claim: A recent model describes a 'mode' that captures behaviour-related dynamics shared between the low- and high-frequency motor cortical LFPs and the neural population activity.
source: Such a relationship has been recently modelled as a 'mode' that captures behaviour-related dynamics that are shared between the low- and high-frequency motor cortical LFPs and the neural population activity (Abbaspourazad et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: The current study presents a novel approach that explicitly quantifies the relationship between each LFP band and the population-wide latent dynamics.
source: Here, we present a novel approach that explicitly quantifies the relationship between each LFP band and the population-wide latent dynamics.
evidence: This describes the methodological contribution of the current study.

claim: Low-frequency LFP bands are correlated with the latent dynamics for each of primary motor, dorsal premotor, and somatosensory cortices.
source: This allows us to show, directly, that low-frequency LFP bands are indeed correlated with the latent dynamics for each of primary motor (Figure 3B), dorsal premotor (Figure 6B), and somatosensory cortices (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles remain stable throughout different processes of behaviour including motor planning.
source: We also extend our investigation beyond movement execution by studying motor planning, to demonstrate that the LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles remain stable throughout different processes of behaviour (Figures 5A, B, 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The robust LFP-latent dynamics correlations during the instructed delay period indicate that their association is not only driven by large common inputs reflecting motor commands but extends to more cognitive processes such as planning an action.
source: This result constitutes an important control. Since there is no overt movement during the planning epoch, the robust LFP-latent dynamics correlations during the instructed delay period indicate that their association is not only driven by large common inputs reflecting motor commands: it extends to more cognitive processes such as planning an action.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings during the planning epoch.

claim: The drop in LFP-latent dynamics correlations during inter-trial intervals suggests that they are a consequence of strong, coordinated synaptic currents across the circuit.
source: This drop suggests that the LFP-latent dynamics correlations are a consequence of strong, coordinated synaptic currents across the circuit.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings during inter-trial intervals.

claim: PMd may retain some aspects of the task during the inter-trial period, as recently shown for the prefrontal cortex (PFC).
source: Interestingly, such a decrease in correlation during the inter-trial period in PMd was not as marked as in M1, perhaps because PMd may retain some aspects of the task during this period, as recently shown for the prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Mehta et al., 2020; Maggi and Humphries, 2022).
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison with previous work on PFC, supported by citations.

claim: PMd activity but not M1 activity reflects the probability of possible upcoming reach directions.
source: Indeed, PMd activity but not M1 activity reflects the probability of possible upcoming reach directions (Glaser et al., 2018), and it also has stronger reward-related signals than M1 (Ramkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on PMd function.

claim: Under the interpretation that PMd retains task aspects during inter-trial periods, 'higher' brain regions such as PFC would be expected to exhibit large LFP-latent dynamics correlations in the absence of overt behaviour, provided that the animal is deliberating or reminiscing.
source: Under this interpretation, we would expect 'higher' brain regions such as PFC to exhibit large LFP-latent dynamics correlations in the absence of overt behaviour, provided that the animal is deliberating or reminiscing.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the interpretation of PMd results.

claim: The stable LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles cannot be predicted based on the relationship between LFPs and single neurons.
source: A critical aspect of our results is that the stable LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles cannot be predicted based on the relationship between LFPs and single neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analyses in Figure 8.

claim: Biophysical models suggest that strong LFP signals may require correlated synaptic inputs to the neurons generating the electric fields.
source: Biophysical models suggest that strong LFP signals may require correlated synaptic inputs to the neurons generating the electric fields, with the spatial extent of such correlated inputs determining the magnitude of the LFP (Lindén et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work on LFP biophysics.

claim: Correlated inputs lead to correlated neural firing patterns that will be captured in the latent dynamics computed with PCA, but much less so in the discharge of any given neuron.
source: These correlated inputs will lead to correlated neural firing patterns that will be captured in the latent dynamics computed with PCA, but much less so in the discharge of any given neuron.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biophysics of LFP generation and PCA methodology.

claim: The finding of robust LFP-latent dynamics correlations is likely driven by the biophysical mechanisms of LFP generation and requires explicitly computing the dominant neural covariance patterns.
source: Thus, our finding of robust LFP-latent dynamics correlations is likely driven by the biophysical mechanisms of LFP generation and requires explicitly computing the dominant neural covariance patterns, since these seem to be largely determined by shared synaptic inputs across the population.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on biophysical principles.

claim: The activity of individual neurons is determined by a high-dimensional set of inputs affecting any given neuron through unknown weights, blurring their relationship with the LFP.
source: In contrast, the activity of individual neurons is determined by a high-dimensional set of inputs affecting any given neuron through unknown weights, blurring their relationship with the LFP.
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of neural computation.

claim: For a given level of correlated synaptic input, the LFP propagates in a frequency-dependent manner, with its spatial reach decreasing quite markedly at higher frequencies.
source: For a given level of correlated synaptic input, the LFP propagates in a frequency-dependent manner, with its spatial reach decreasing quite markedly at higher frequencies (Łęski et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work on LFP biophysics.

claim: High-frequency components, especially broadband signals at frequencies >50 Hz, seem to reflect local neural spiking.
source: Yet, high-frequency components, especially broadband signals at frequencies >50 Hz, seem also to reflect local neural spiking (Ray and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The robust associations defining the roughly V-shaped LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles may have two different sources: at low frequencies, they may be dominated by correlated synaptic inputs; at high frequencies, they may reflect a combination of correlated synaptic input and more local neural spiking.
source: It is thus possible that the robust associations defining our roughly V-shaped LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles (Figures 3B, 6B and 7B) have two different sources: at low frequencies, they may be dominated by the correlated synaptic inputs leading to the emergence of low-dimensional latent dynamics in the sensorimotor cortices during behaviour; at high frequencies, they may reflect a combination of correlated synaptic input across the population and more local neural spiking.
evidence: This is a speculation based on biophysical understanding and the observed correlation profiles.

claim: 'Multi-unit' firing rates at 100–200 Hz and 200–400 Hz are more strongly correlated with the LFPs than single neuron firings rates.
source: In agreement with this, 'multi-unit' firing rates at 100–200 Hz and 200–400 Hz are more strongly correlated with the LFPs than single neuron firings rates (Bansal et al., 2012; Perel et al., 2015) (compare Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1D), although still less so than the LFP-latent dynamics (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 8 and supplementary figures.

claim: The importance of circuit biophysics in determining the LFP properties may explain the differences in LFP-latent dynamics correlations across regions.
source: Together with functional specialisation, the importance of circuit biophysics in determining the LFP properties may also explain the differences in LFP-latent dynamics correlations across regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the region-specific findings.

claim: Each of the three cortical regions studied has different neuron types, layer organisation, and local and long-range connectivity patterns, all of which influence the biophysics of LFP generation.
source: Likely due to their varying evolutionary past (Kaas, 2004), each of the three cortical regions we studied has different neuron types, layer organisation, and local and long-range connectivity patterns (Harris and Shepherd, 2015), all of which influence the biophysics of LFP generation (Einevoll et al., 2013; Lindén et al., 2011; Buzsáki et al., 2012; Łęski et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on cortical architecture and LFP biophysics.

claim: It is reasonable for the 'mapping' between latent dynamics and LFPs to be region-dependent due to differences in circuit biophysics.
source: Because of this, it is reasonable for the 'mapping' between latent dynamics and LFPs captured by our correlation profiles to be region-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on known differences in cortical architecture.

claim: The most striking difference in LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles across regions appears at the mid-range 12–25 Hz band.
source: The most striking difference in LFP-latent dynamics correlation profiles across regions appears at the mid-range 12–25 Hz band.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing results across regions.

claim: There is not a clear rostro-caudal gradient in the LFP-latent dynamics relationship at 12–25 Hz; instead, the correlation is high in PMd and even higher in area 2, but extremely low in the intermediately located M1.
source: Surprisingly, there is not a clear rostro-caudal gradient in their relationship; instead, the correlation is high in PMd (Figure 6B) and even higher in area 2 (Figure 7B), but extremely low in the intermediately located M1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing results across regions, shown in multiple figures.

claim: Across all three regions, the 12–25 Hz band is never a good predictor of movement parameters, even when the LFP-latent dynamics correlations reach 0.5–0.6.
source: What is common across all three regions is that the 12–25 Hz band is never a good predictor of movement parameters, even when the LFP-latent dynamics correlations reach 0.5–0.6 (Figures 4C and 6E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing decoding results across regions, shown in multiple figures.

claim: The lack of correlation between 12–25 Hz LFP and movement parameters is consistent with studies of M1 LFPs during movement.
source: This lack of correlation with movement parameters is consistent with studies of M1 LFPs during movement (Sanes and Donoghue, 1993; Murthy and Fetz, 1996a), which describe a marked decrease in LFP 12–25 Hz power prior to movement initiation (Sanes and Donoghue, 1993; Perel et al., 2015; Donoghue et al., 1998; Witham et al., 2007), with some transient oscillations only during specific tasks.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on M1 LFPs.

claim: 12–25 Hz oscillations often appear when monkeys pick up treats, explore their surroundings, or perform relatively challenging finger tasks, but are very rare during more 'automatic' wrist tasks.
source: These oscillations often appear when monkeys pick up treats, explore their surroundings, or perform relatively challenging finger tasks, but are very rare during more 'automatic' wrist tasks (Sanes and Donoghue, 1993; Baker et al., 1997; Murthy and Fetz, 1996a) – the latter being most similar to the centre-out reaching task we studied.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on motor cortex oscillations.

claim: The 12–25 Hz LFP band may be a by-product of population activity related to attention or other high-level cognitive features such as keeping track of task structure.
source: Combined, these observations suggest that the 12–25 Hz LFP band may be a by-product of population activity related to attention (Murthy and Fetz, 1996a) or other high-level cognitive features such as keeping track of task structure.
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous work and the current findings.

claim: 12–25 Hz LFP power could potentially be driven by the activity of neural populations in regions projecting to the sensorimotor cortices, rather than by the activity of local populations.
source: As such, 12–25 Hz LFP power could potentially be driven by the activity of neural populations in regions projecting to the sensorimotor cortices, rather than by the activity of local populations (Herreras, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation based on understanding of LFP generation, supported by a citation.

claim: LFP 12–25 Hz power in PFC modulates as monkeys select between stimulus-response rules, suggesting that PMd 12–25 Hz oscillations could be correlated with task structure.
source: Indeed, LFP 12–25 Hz power in PFC modulates as monkeys select between stimulus-response rules (Buschman et al., 2012), suggesting that PMd 12–25 Hz oscillations could be correlated with task structure.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and used to support a speculation about PMd.

claim: Parietal cortical LFP 12–25 Hz power changes as monkeys choose between movement types based on visual cues, suggesting a potential origin of area 2 12–25 Hz oscillations related to task structure.
source: Analogously, parietal cortical LFP 12–25 Hz power changes as monkeys choose between movement types based on visual cues (Scherberger et al., 2005), again suggesting a potential origin of area 2 12–25 Hz oscillations related to task structure.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and used to support a speculation about area 2.

claim: LFPs are fundamentally related to the shared patterns that dominate the activity of a neural population, rather than to the activity of the neurons themselves.
source: Yet, the relationship between the LFPs and the activity of neurons driving behaviour has remained elusive. Here, we show that, likely due to the biophysics of their generation, LFPs are fundamentally related to the shared patterns that dominate the activity of a neural population, rather than to the activity of the neurons themselves.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the findings.

claim: While the frequency-dependent association between LFPs and latent dynamics varies across the sensorimotor cortex, for a given cortical region and frequency band it is stable throughout the behaviour.
source: While this frequency-dependent association varies across the sensorimotor cortex, for a given cortical region and frequency band it is stable throughout the behaviour.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the findings.

claim: The approach will likely uncover stable LFP-latent dynamics correlations not only within the sensorimotor cortices but beyond, as low-dimensional latent dynamics have been found across many cortical and subcortical brain regions.
source: We anticipate that our approach will uncover stable LFP-latent dynamics correlations not only within the sensorimotor cortices but beyond, as low-dimensional latent dynamics have been found across many cortical and subcortical brain regions (Gallego et al., 2017; Keemink and Machens, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Stable LFP-latent dynamic correlations are expected during cognitive tasks, since the two are correlated during 'abstract' movement planning.
source: We further expect to uncover stable LFP-latent dynamic correlations during cognitive tasks, since the two are correlated during 'abstract' movement planning.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings during movement planning.

claim: Identifying LFP-latent dynamics relationships offers an exciting opportunity to integrate studies based on either type of signals, including a large body of field recordings in neurological patients.
source: Identifying these relationships offers an exciting opportunity to integrate studies based on either type of signals, including a large body of field recordings in neurological patients (Kelley et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2017; Vaz et al., 2019; Anumanchipalli et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018a; Méndez-Bértolo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings, supported by citations to clinical studies.
